questions.hook: He fainted on the stairs. That single detail decides the question.
questions.key_finding: Carotid upstroke: delayed and low amplitude
questions.short_vignette: A 74-year-old man collapses while climbing the stairs and recovers within a minute. He has a harsh systolic murmur at the right upper sternal border radiating to both carotids, and a delayed, low-amplitude carotid upstroke.
questions.vignette: A 74-year-old man comes to the clinic because of a 6-month history of shortness of breath with exertion. Last week he lost consciousness while climbing the stairs to his apartment and recovered within a minute. He has no chest pain. Blood pressure 128/76 mmHg, pulse 72/min. Cardiac examination shows a harsh, crescendo-decrescendo systolic murmur loudest at the right second intercostal space, radiating to both carotid arteries. The second heart sound is soft. The carotid upstroke is delayed and low in amplitude. The lungs are clear and there is no peripheral edema.
questions.stem: Which of the following best explains this patient's loss of consciousness?

options.text: Fixed stroke volume limiting the rise in cardiac output during exertion
options.why: A stenotic valve cannot open wider when demand rises. At rest the stiff ventricle still generates adequate output; on exertion stroke volume is capped, cardiac output fails to rise, and cerebral perfusion falls.
options.would_make_right: Nothing - this is the correct mechanism for exertional syncope with a fixed outflow obstruction.

options.why: Calcific aortic stenosis can extend into the conduction system, but a block is not load-dependent and does not wait for the stairs.
options.would_make_right: Syncope occurring at rest, or an ECG showing wide-complex bradycardia with absent P waves.

options.text: Ventricular arrhythmia arising from myocardial scar
options.why: Arrhythmic syncope classically has no warning and no reproducible exertional trigger. This patient's syncope is exertion-linked, which points to a haemodynamic cause.
options.would_make_right: Syncope without prodrome, family history of sudden cardiac death, scar on echocardiography, or a prolonged QT interval.

options.text: Vasovagal reflex triggered by increased intrathoracic pressure
options.why: Vasovagal syncope has a prodrome of warmth, nausea and tunnel vision, is provoked by heat, pain or prolonged standing, and does not produce a fixed low-amplitude carotid upstroke.
options.would_make_right: A clear prodrome, syncope while standing, rapid full recovery, and a normal cardiac examination.

options.text: Orthostatic hypotension from reduced intravascular volume
options.why: There is no volume loss, no diuretic use, and no positional trigger. Orthostatic syncope occurs within seconds of standing, not after climbing stairs.
options.would_make_right: A documented postural blood pressure drop, diuretic use or dehydration, and syncope on standing.

questions.rule: Exertional syncope is a haemodynamic problem until proven otherwise: the heart cannot meet demand. Aortic stenosis, hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and pulmonary hypertension are the three causes.
sources: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1, Cardiology - Valvular disease
2020 ACC/AHA Guideline for the Management of Patients With Valvular Heart Disease

questions.hook: A 95% sensitive test. An 8.8% chance you actually have the disease.
questions.short_vignette: A screening test has 95% sensitivity and 90% specificity. The disease affects 1% of the population. A patient tests positive.
questions.vignette: A new screening test for a disease has a sensitivity of 95% and a specificity of 90%. The disease has a prevalence of 1% in the population being screened.
questions.stem: If a person from this population tests positive, what is the probability that they actually have the disease?

options.why: In 10,000 people, 100 have the disease and 95 of those test positive; of the 9,900 without disease, 990 test positive falsely. Of 1,085 positives only 95 are true, giving 95/1,085 = 8.8%.
options.would_make_right: Nothing - this is the correct predictive value at 1% prevalence.

options.why: This is the sensitivity, which answers the opposite question: among people who have the disease, what fraction test positive.
options.would_make_right: A question asking for the proportion of diseased patients who test positive, not the proportion of positives who are diseased.

options.why: This is the specificity: among people who are well, what fraction test negative. It ignores prevalence and runs in the wrong direction.
options.would_make_right: A question asking what fraction of healthy people test negative.

options.why: A 50% positive predictive value would require prevalence high enough to balance the false positive rate. At 1% prevalence the false positives swamp the true positives.
options.would_make_right: A prevalence roughly equal to the false positive rate, which at these test characteristics is about 10%.

options.why: This is the false positive rate applied to the whole population, not a predictive value. It answers no question that was asked.
options.would_make_right: A question asking for the probability that a healthy person tests positive, which is 10% here, not 0.9%.

questions.rule: Sensitivity and specificity belong to the test. Predictive values belong to the patient in front of you, and they move with prevalence. Never answer a predictive-value question before writing down the prevalence.
sources: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1, Biostatistics - Sensitivity, specificity, predictive values

questions.hook: Platelets 18,000. Every instinct says transfuse. That instinct is wrong.
questions.short_vignette: A 29-year-old woman has five days of bruising and confusion. Platelets 18,000, haemoglobin 7.4, schistocytes on the smear, PT and aPTT both normal, creatinine 1.1.
questions.vignette: A 29-year-old woman comes in with five days of fatigue and easy bruising, and her husband says she has been confused since this morning. Temperature 37.8 C. There are petechiae over both shins. She is not pregnant and takes no medications. Hemoglobin 7.4 g/dL, platelets 18,000/uL, reticulocytes 9%, lactate dehydrogenase 900 U/L, indirect bilirubin 2.4 mg/dL, creatinine 1.1 mg/dL. PT/INR and aPTT are both normal. Peripheral smear shows schistocytes. Urinalysis shows 1+ protein and no red cells.
questions.stem: Which of the following is the most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.why: Plasma exchange removes the autoantibody against ADAMTS13 and replaces the enzyme at the same time. Untreated TTP carries high mortality and the response window is measured in hours.
options.would_make_right: Nothing - plasma exchange is first-line for suspected TTP with neurologic involvement.

options.why: Every transfused platelet is fuel for further microthrombi. Platelet transfusion is contraindicated in TTP unless there is life-threatening bleeding or imminent surgery.
options.would_make_right: Active life-threatening haemorrhage, intracranial bleeding, or a patient going to the operating room immediately.

options.why: Eculizumab blocks complement C5 and treats atypical haemolytic uraemic syndrome, which is renal-predominant with a rising creatinine and normal ADAMTS13 activity. This patient's creatinine is 1.1.
options.would_make_right: Renal-predominant disease with rapidly rising creatinine, dialysis requirement, and normal ADAMTS13 activity.

options.why: Vitamin K treats coagulopathy, which prolongs the PT. This patient's PT and aPTT are both normal, so there is no coagulation factor deficiency to correct.
options.would_make_right: A prolonged PT or INR, as in warfarin use, liver disease or fat malabsorption.

options.why: TTP is a medical emergency. Observation without plasma exchange was associated with mortality above 90% historically and remains unacceptable today.
options.would_make_right: A stable patient with no red cell destruction, which is not this picture.

questions.rule: Microangiopathic haemolysis plus thrombocytopenia plus normal coagulation studies equals a thrombotic microangiopathy. Platelets are contraindicated and plasma exchange is the treatment: today, not tomorrow.
sources: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1, Hematology - Thrombotic microangiopathies
ISTH Guidelines for the Management of Thrombotic Thrombocytopenic Purpura

questions.hook: It says to wait for antibiotics—so you order cultures after starting them, right?
questions.vignette: A 62-year-old man with a history of aortic valve replacement presents with 2 days of fever and chills. He is hypotensive and tachycardic. Vitals: T 39.6°C, HR 118/min, BP 92/58 mmHg, RR 22/min. Labs: WBC 15,200/mm3. Two sets of blood cultures are drawn. He receives empiric IV antibiotics immediately afterward. Cultures later grow gram-positive cocci in clusters. Which next action best improves diagnostic yield while also addressing sepsis?
questions.short_vignette: Man with suspected endocarditis: after drawing cultures and starting antibiotics, what improves diagnostic yield?
questions.stem: To maximize the likelihood of identifying the causative organism in suspected infective endocarditis, what should be done regarding blood cultures and antibiotics?

options.text: Obtain multiple blood cultures before giving any antibiotics
options.why: Culturing before antimicrobial therapy maximizes the chance that organisms will grow. In suspected infective endocarditis with sepsis, draw cultures urgently and then start empiric antibiotics without delay.
options.would_make_right: Change the vignette so antibiotics are started before blood cultures are drawn; then correct it by specifying cultures are obtained immediately before antibiotics.

options.text: Start antibiotics immediately and delay blood cultures until vitals stabilize
options.why: Antibiotics rapidly reduce culture positivity. Delaying cultures lowers diagnostic yield and risks missing the opportunity to isolate the pathogen, which is crucial in endocarditis.
options.would_make_right: Alter the vignette so blood cultures were drawn only after several hours of antibiotics and then choose the corrected approach of drawing cultures before antibiotics.

options.text: Order only a single blood culture set because endocarditis is persistent
options.why: Bacteremia can be intermittent; multiple sets from different venipuncture sites increase the probability of capturing organisms. A single set risks false-negative results.
options.would_make_right: Change the vignette to include only one blood culture set; then make the correct option correct by revising it to multiple sets drawn before antibiotics.

options.text: Use transthoracic echocardiography first and skip blood cultures since echo detects infection
options.why: Echocardiography supports diagnosis but does not identify the organism. Blood cultures are essential to guide targeted therapy and determine the causative pathogen.
options.would_make_right: Revise the vignette to state that blood cultures are not obtained; then the correct action becomes obtaining blood cultures promptly before antibiotics.

options.text: Discontinue antibiotics after cultures are drawn because the organism will regrow
options.why: Stopping antibiotics after cultures does not reliably allow regrowth and is dangerous in septic patients. Ongoing therapy is required while culture results and susceptibilities are pending.
options.would_make_right: Modify the vignette to say antibiotics are stopped after cultures; then the corrected diagnostic-yield strategy would still require starting only after cultures are drawn and continuing empiric therapy.

questions.rule: In suspected infective endocarditis, draw multiple blood cultures urgently before starting antibiotics to preserve culture yield while treating sepsis immediately afterward.
sources: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 - Infectious Disease/Endocarditis
IDSA Infective Endocarditis guideline (blood culture timing)

questions.hook: He says, 'My son’s bruises started after a dental procedure—so he must have von Willebrand disease,' right?
questions.key_finding: Prolonged isolated aPTT with normal platelets
questions.vignette: A 6-year-old boy is brought for frequent bruising and prolonged bleeding from minor cuts. His mother reports that after dental work 2 weeks ago, he had persistent gum bleeding for 2 days. He has no epistaxis or petechiae. Vitals are normal. Exam shows large ecchymoses on the legs. CBC shows platelets 240,000/mm3. PT is 11.2 seconds (normal). aPTT is 68 seconds (markedly prolonged). Mixing study fails to correct. No joint deformities are noted yet. The child is otherwise healthy.
questions.short_vignette: 6-year-old boy with large bruises and prolonged post-dental bleeding; platelets normal; PT normal; isolated prolonged aPTT not corrected by mixing.
questions.stem: Which diagnosis best explains the coagulation abnormality?

options.text: Hemophilia A due to factor VIII deficiency
options.why: Hemophilia A causes impaired intrinsic pathway clotting, leading to an isolated prolonged aPTT with normal platelet count and PT. Failure of a mixing study to correct suggests a true factor deficiency pattern consistent with hemophilia rather than factor inhibitor presence.
options.would_make_right: Add a history of similar bleeding in maternal relatives and specify that aPTT does not correct with mixing due to factor VIII deficiency (not an inhibitor).

options.why: von Willebrand disease typically presents with mucocutaneous bleeding (epistaxis, gum bleeding, menorrhagia) and often shows prolonged bleeding time with variable aPTT prolongation. It would not classically produce a markedly prolonged isolated aPTT with normal PT and normal platelets as the primary abnormality.
options.would_make_right: Change the vignettes bleeding pattern to include recurrent epistaxis and note decreased von Willebrand factor activity with reduced factor VIII secondary effects.

options.why: Glanzmann thrombasthenia is a platelet function disorder with normal PT and typically normal or mildly affected aPTT, not a markedly prolonged isolated aPTT. It causes mucocutaneous bleeding with normal platelet counts but impaired aggregation.
options.would_make_right: Keep PT and aPTT normal but add painless mucosal bleeding with normal platelet count and abnormal platelet aggregation testing.

options.text: Acquired hemophilia due to factor VIII inhibitor
options.why: Acquired hemophilia usually occurs in older adults or postpartum and causes severe bleeding with a prolonged aPTT that does not correct on mixing due to an inhibitor. The patient is a young boy with no trigger described, making inherited hemophilia more likely.
options.would_make_right: Change the patient to a 70-year-old (or postpartum patient) and add a new, sudden onset of bleeding with no family history, consistent with an acquired inhibitor.

options.why: DIC typically causes thrombocytopenia and both PT and aPTT prolongation due to consumption of multiple clotting factors. This patient has normal platelets and a normal PT, arguing strongly against DIC.
options.would_make_right: Lower platelets to ~30,000/mm3 and prolong PT as well (eg, both PT and aPTT markedly increased) with clinical sepsis or trauma.

questions.rule: Isolated prolonged aPTT with normal PT and normal platelets points to intrinsic factor problems (eg hemophilia) rather than platelet disorders or vitamin K deficiency.
sources: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 - Coagulation Disorders
UpToDate review of hemophilia and mixing studies

questions.hook: Proteinuria alone is not enough—spot the missing criterion for preeclampsia.
questions.vignette: A 29-year-old G2P1 woman at 28 weeks’ gestation presents with headache and mild swelling of her face. Blood pressure is 162/104 mmHg on two measurements 4 hours apart. Urinalysis shows protein 1+ with a urine protein-to-creatinine ratio of 0.3. Serum creatinine is 0.8 mg/dL. Platelets are 240,000/µL. AST is 22 U/L and ALT is 24 U/L. She has no right upper quadrant pain and no visual changes. What is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.short_vignette: At 28 weeks, BP 162/104 mmHg with urine protein/Cr 0.3 and normal platelets/AST/ALT/creatinine.
questions.stem: At 28 weeks’ gestation, she has new-onset hypertension but no evidence of end-organ dysfunction; what is the most likely diagnosis?

options.why: Preeclampsia requires hypertension after 20 weeks plus proteinuria meeting threshold or end-organ dysfunction (eg, thrombocytopenia, elevated transaminases, renal insufficiency, pulmonary edema, or persistent neurologic symptoms). Her protein-to-creatinine ratio is below the diagnostic cutoff and labs are normal.
options.would_make_right: Increase urine protein-to-creatinine ratio to ≥0.3 with a clearly measured quantitative protein level, or add end-organ findings such as platelets 90,000/µL or creatinine 1.1 mg/dL.

options.why: Gestational hypertension is new-onset hypertension after 20 weeks without proteinuria meeting criteria and without end-organ dysfunction. Her protein/Cr ratio is 0.3 and she has normal platelets, creatinine, and transaminases.
options.would_make_right: Change the urine protein-to-creatinine ratio to 0.1 (or remove proteinuria findings) while keeping BP and end-organ labs the same.

options.why: Chronic hypertension is present before 20 weeks or before pregnancy is known to have started, or persists beyond 12 weeks postpartum. This case begins at 28 weeks.
options.would_make_right: Specify that her blood pressure was ≥140/90 mmHg before 20 weeks’ gestation or earlier in the current pregnancy.

options.why: HELLP requires hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets. She has normal platelets and normal transaminases, with no evidence of hemolysis.
options.would_make_right: Lower platelets to <100,000/µL and elevate AST/ALT to >2× the upper limit, adding hemolysis markers (eg, elevated LDH and schistocytes).

options.why: This condition typically presents in the third trimester with hepatic dysfunction (markedly elevated transaminases), coagulopathy, and sometimes hypoglycemia. Her AST/ALT are normal and no coagulopathy is provided.
options.would_make_right: Add hepatic failure clues such as AST/ALT significantly elevated with an INR elevation (or hypoglycemia) while keeping hypertension present.

questions.rule: In pregnancy, diagnose preeclampsia only when hypertension after 20 weeks is accompanied by significant proteinuria and/or end-organ dysfunction.
sources: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 - Obstetrics: Preeclampsia and Gestational Hypertension
ACOG Practice Bulletin (Preeclampsia and Related Disorders)

questions.hook: He says, “My kidneys will be fine again once I stop the medication,” but what do labs show?
questions.key_finding: Low FENa with high urine osmolality
questions.vignette: A 68-year-old man with chronic heart failure presents with 2 days of poor oral intake and dizziness after starting a new diuretic. He has dry mucous membranes. Vitals: BP 88/54 mmHg, HR 102/min, RR 18/min, T 36.8°C. Labs show creatinine 2.1 mg/dL (baseline 1.0) and BUN 42 mg/dL. Urinalysis shows no casts. Urine studies: urine sodium 18 mEq/L, urine osmolality 620 mOsm/kg. After IV fluids, his urine output improves over several hours.
questions.short_vignette: Elderly on diuretics with dehydration: creatinine up, no casts. Urine Na low (18), urine osm high (620) after fluids improve output.
questions.stem: Which interpretation best explains his acute kidney injury?

options.text: Prerenal azotemia from decreased renal perfusion
options.why: Prerenal AKI is characterized by intact tubular function, leading to avid sodium and water reabsorption. Low urine sodium and high urine osmolality support this.
options.would_make_right: Change urine sodium to 18 mEq/L (already low) and add “no granular casts” to the urinalysis; keep dehydration and hypotension unchanged.

options.text: Acute tubular necrosis from nephrotoxin injury
options.why: ATN typically causes impaired tubular sodium reabsorption, yielding higher urine sodium and often granular casts. This patient’s urine sodium is low and urinalysis shows no casts.
options.would_make_right: Replace urine sodium 18 mEq/L with 60 mEq/L and add “muddy brown granular casts” to urinalysis; keep hypotension history but remove dehydration as the dominant finding.

options.why: Postrenal AKI often presents with urinary retention symptoms or flank pain and can show hydronephrosis. The vignette emphasizes dehydration/hypotension and shows rapid improvement with fluids.
options.would_make_right: Add decreased urine output with suprapubic fullness and flank pain; include renal ultrasound showing bilateral hydronephrosis.

options.why: Intrinsic glomerular disease would more likely produce hematuria with dysmorphic RBCs or RBC casts and proteinuria. Urinalysis here shows no casts and no hematuria is described.
options.would_make_right: Add urinalysis with “RBC casts and dysmorphic RBCs” plus proteinuria; do not include the dehydration/hypotension response to fluids.

options.text: Renal artery stenosis causing ischemic nephropathy
options.why: Renal artery stenosis often presents with refractory hypertension and can show asymmetric kidney size or elevated renovascular indices. This patient is hypotensive with dehydration and improves with volume repletion.
options.would_make_right: Change BP to 170/96 mmHg and add “abdominal bruit” with ultrasound showing small, atrophic kidney; remove the poor oral intake/dehydration narrative.

questions.rule: Low urine sodium with concentrated urine suggests prerenal azotemia; ATN shows higher urine sodium and casts.
sources: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 - Renal Physiology
FENa interpretation (prerenal vs ATN) and urine concentration/casts

questions.hook: She has hyperkalemia and low sodium—don't confuse Addison disease with adrenal crisis from secondary causes.
questions.vignette: A 42-year-old woman with progressive fatigue and weight loss reports dizziness when standing. She also has nausea and craving salt. Exam shows mild hyperpigmentation of the knuckles. Vitals: BP 86/54 mmHg, HR 102/min. Labs: Na 128 mEq/L, K 6.1 mEq/L, glucose 68 mg/dL. Morning serum cortisol is 4.2 µg/dL. Plasma ACTH is 860 pg/mL.
questions.short_vignette: Hypotension, hyperpigmentation, Na 128, K 6.1, cortisol 4.2; ACTH 860.
questions.stem: Which endocrine diagnosis best explains her laboratory pattern?

options.why: Primary adrenal failure lowers cortisol, removing negative feedback and causing markedly elevated ACTH. High ACTH also drives increased melanocyte stimulation, explaining hyperpigmentation.
options.would_make_right: Change the vignette to describe chronic adrenal destruction and keep ACTH markedly elevated with low cortisol.

options.text: Secondary adrenal insufficiency due to pituitary failure
options.why: Secondary causes reduce cortisol but do not significantly increase ACTH, so hyperpigmentation would be absent and hyperkalemia would be less prominent.
options.would_make_right: Replace the ACTH result with low or normal ACTH (e.g., ACTH 10 pg/mL) while keeping low cortisol.

options.why: Thyroid storm causes hyperthermia, tachycardia, and agitation; it does not cause the specific cortisol–ACTH pattern or hyperkalemia from aldosterone deficiency.
options.would_make_right: Change the vignette to include fever and severe tachyarrhythmia with normal electrolytes and a normal cortisol/ACTH pattern.

options.why: Pheochromocytoma presents with episodic hypertension, palpitations, and diaphoresis; it does not produce low cortisol with elevated ACTH or hyperpigmentation.
options.would_make_right: Add paroxysmal headaches and sustained hypertension with normal sodium and potassium and remove cortisol/ACTH abnormalities.

options.text: Congenital adrenal hyperplasia due to 21-hydroxylase deficiency
options.why: Classic 21-hydroxylase deficiency often causes androgen excess and typically presents earlier in life; the vignette describes adult-onset symptoms without virilization or androgen-related findings.
options.would_make_right: Add a history of childhood onset with signs of androgen excess (eg, early pubarche/virilization) while keeping cortisol low and ACTH high.

questions.rule: Low cortisol with high ACTH and hyperpigmentation indicates primary adrenal insufficiency.
sources: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 - Endocrine (Adrenal Cortex Disorders)
Guideline: Endocrine Society clinical guidance on adrenal insufficiency diagnosis (ACTH/cortisol interpretation)

questions.hook: He says his new thirst proves type 2 diabetes, but consider ketones instead?
questions.vignette: A 19-year-old man presents with 1 week of increasing thirst, frequent urination, and unintentional weight loss. He has nausea and abdominal discomfort. Vitals show BP 118/72 mmHg, HR 112/min, RR 24/min, and T 37.0°C. Labs: glucose 465 mg/dL, serum bicarbonate 13 mEq/L, anion gap 22 mEq/L, and beta-hydroxybutyrate elevated. Serum potassium is 5.1 mEq/L. Urinalysis shows glucose and ketones. What is the most likely pathophysiologic defect driving his condition?
questions.short_vignette: 19-year-old with glucose 465, anion gap metabolic acidosis, and elevated beta-hydroxybutyrate.
questions.stem: Which defect best explains his current presentation?

options.text: Autoimmune destruction of pancreatic beta cells
options.why: Type 1 diabetes causes insulin deficiency leading to increased lipolysis, ketone production, and an anion gap metabolic acidosis. The presence of ketonemia in a young patient with rapid symptom onset supports this mechanism.
options.would_make_right: Change the age to a teenager and add history of autoimmune disease (eg, elevated anti-GAD antibodies) while keeping ketonemia and anion gap acidosis.

options.text: Insulin receptor resistance causing impaired glucose uptake
options.why: Insulin resistance in type 2 diabetes typically does not cause ketonemia with anion gap metabolic acidosis unless there is severe stress or profound insulin deficiency. The vignette emphasizes active ketone production.
options.would_make_right: Remove ketones and replace beta-hydroxybutyrate with normal values, while describing longer, less acute symptoms more consistent with type 2 diabetes.

options.text: Defective insulin secretion with preserved insulin action
options.why: Partial insulin secretory defects without severe insulin deficiency usually do not produce marked ketonemia and anion gap metabolic acidosis. The vignette already demonstrates significant absolute insulin lack physiology.
options.would_make_right: Lower glucose substantially (eg, ~180-250 mg/dL) and change beta-hydroxybutyrate to normal, while describing stable weight without acute acidosis.

options.text: Excess cortisol production leading to increased gluconeogenesis
options.why: Cortisol excess causes hyperglycemia via gluconeogenesis but does not primarily lead to ketonemia with anion gap metabolic acidosis in this presentation. The key abnormality is ketone-driven acidosis from insulin deficiency.
options.would_make_right: Add physical findings of Cushing syndrome (eg, proximal muscle weakness, moon facies) and replace ketonemia with elevated cortisol/low ACTH while normalizing anion gap.

options.text: Increased glucagon secretion causing hepatic glycogenolysis
options.why: Glucagon excess can raise blood glucose, but it is not the typical mechanism for ketonemia and anion gap metabolic acidosis caused by insulin deficiency. No findings suggest a glucagon-secreting tumor or similar process.
options.would_make_right: Include a pancreatic mass with markedly elevated glucagon levels and remove ketones/anion gap acidosis, leaving isolated hyperglycemia.

questions.rule: In acute symptomatic hyperglycemia, ketonemia with anion gap acidosis points to absolute insulin deficiency (type 1).
sources: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 - Endocrine (Diabetes Mellitus) and Biochemistry/Pathology (Anion gap metabolic acidosis)
ADA Standards of Care (DKA diagnostic features)

questions.hook: “Why does this patient have a diastolic murmur that gets louder when the heart rate slows?”
questions.vignette: A 68-year-old woman presents with progressive dyspnea on exertion and orthopnea for 6 months. She reports palpitations but no chest pain. Vitals: BP 128/76 mmHg, HR 86/min, RR 18/min, SpO2 94% on room air. Cardiac exam shows an irregularly irregular rhythm. A low-pitched, mid-diastolic murmur is heard best at the cardiac apex with the patient in the left lateral position. An additional high-frequency sound follows S2. Transthoracic echocardiography shows thickened mitral valve leaflets with restricted opening. What maneuver will most increase the murmur’s intensity?
questions.short_vignette: 68F with dyspnea, AF, apex mid-diastolic rumble plus opening snap; echo shows restricted mitral leaflet opening. Which maneuver increases murmur intensity?
questions.stem: Which maneuver would most increase the intensity of her murmur?

options.why: Squatting increases systemic vascular resistance and increases venous return, raising left atrial pressure and transmit flow across a stenotic mitral valve, making the diastolic murmur louder.
options.would_make_right: Change the vignette to state the murmur is a mitral stenosis diastolic rumble with opening snap, then ask specifically for a maneuver that increases venous return/left atrial pressure (squatting).

options.why: Standing decreases venous return, lowering left atrial pressure and reducing flow across the stenotic mitral valve, so the murmur would lessen.
options.would_make_right: If squatting (A) were replaced by standing (B) in the question with the same vignette, B would become correct.

options.text: Instructing her to perform a Valsalva maneuver
options.why: Valsalva decreases venous return (especially with strain), reducing mitral flow and diminishing the intensity of the diastolic murmur.
options.would_make_right: If the vignette’s question instead asked for a maneuver that decreases venous return, then Valsalva would be the correct choice.

options.text: Administering a beta-agonist that increases heart rate
options.why: In mitral stenosis, tachycardia shortens diastole, reducing time for blood to flow across the stenotic valve, so the murmur becomes softer.
options.would_make_right: If the vignette asked which intervention decreases murmur intensity in mitral stenosis, then increasing heart rate would be correct.

options.why: Reducing preload lowers left atrial pressure and mitral transvalvular flow, which would weaken the murmur rather than increase it.
options.would_make_right: If the vignette asked which maneuver decreases murmur intensity, nitrate-induced preload reduction would make E correct.

questions.rule: In mitral stenosis, maneuvers that increase left atrial pressure or prolong diastole increase the murmur intensity.
sources: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 - Cardiology: Valvular Heart Disease
ACC/AHA guideline discussion of physical exam maneuvers for valvular lesions

review.hook: “My wedding ring won’t fit anymore—could this be thyroid hormone?”
review.vignette: A 48-year-old man reports enlargement of his hands and feet over 3 years. He also developed thickened facial features and increased shoe size. He complains of new headaches and blurred peripheral vision. On exam, he has prognathism and coarse facial features. Blood pressure is 148/92 mmHg, pulse 82/min, and temperature 36.8°C. MRI shows a sellar mass compressing the optic chiasm. Laboratory testing reveals elevated IGF-1 at 840 ng/mL (reference 90–250). Serum TSH is normal and free T4 is normal. Which underlying process best explains his condition?
review.short_vignette: 48M with enlarged hands, headaches, visual field symptoms, sellar mass, and high IGF-1 with normal thyroid tests—what causes it?
review.stem: Which underlying process best explains his condition?

options.text: Pituitary somatotroph tumor secreting excess GH
options.why: Acromegaly is due to excess growth hormone from a pituitary adenoma, leading to increased IGF-1. Elevated IGF-1 with a sellar mass and compressive symptoms is decisive.
options.would_make_right: Keep the sellar mass and add that the patient’s GH is inappropriately elevated for the time of day.

options.text: Autonomous activation of thyroid hormone receptors in peripheral tissues
options.why: Thyroid hormone excess would affect thyroid labs (↑ free T4 and often suppressed TSH). The vignette explicitly shows normal TSH and normal free T4.
options.would_make_right: Replace the normal thyroid tests with elevated free T4 and suppressed TSH.

options.text: Ectopic secretion of GH-releasing hormone by a small cell lung tumor
options.why: Ectopic GH-releasing hormone is uncommon and would not produce a sellar mass compressing the optic chiasm. The imaging finding localizes the source to the pituitary.
options.would_make_right: Remove the sellar mass and add CT findings of a lung mass with elevated GH-releasing hormone.

options.text: Deficiency of pituitary growth hormone leading to reduced IGF-1
options.why: Growth hormone deficiency would lower IGF-1 rather than elevate it. The patient has classic acromegalic changes with elevated IGF-1.
options.would_make_right: Change IGF-1 to below reference and MRI to show a non-secreting or damaged pituitary without mass effect.

options.text: Excess adrenal cortisol causing acromegaly-like body changes
options.why: Cushing syndrome features centripetal obesity, striae, and glucose/cortisol-related findings, not a sellar mass with increased IGF-1. The vignette lacks cortisol features and shows a GH–IGF-1 pattern.
options.would_make_right: Add Cushingoid exam findings (eg, wide purple striae) and provide evidence of hypercortisolism (eg, elevated late-night salivary cortisol).

review.rule: In suspected acromegaly, elevated IGF-1 plus pituitary mass effect points to a GH-secreting pituitary adenoma.
sources: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 - Endocrine (Pituitary Disorders)
Endocrine Society clinical practice guidance (Acromegaly)

review.topic: Acute Coronary Syndrome: NSTEMI vs Unstable Angina
review.hook: You can’t assume chest pain with no ST elevation is unstable angina—troponin decides NSTEMI.
review.vignette: A 58-year-old man with hypertension presents to the ED with 40 minutes of substernal chest pressure at rest. He is diaphoretic and nauseated. Vitals: BP 146/88 mmHg, HR 104/min, RR 20/min, SpO2 98% on room air, T 36.8°C. ECG shows 1 mm ST depression in leads V4-V6 without ST-segment elevation. Serum high-sensitivity troponin I returns at 0.9 ng/mL (reference <0.04 ng/mL). What diagnosis best fits this presentation?
review.short_vignette: 58M with rest chest pressure, ST depression (no ST elevation), high-sensitivity troponin I elevated to 0.9 ng/mL.
review.stem: Which diagnosis best explains his presentation?

options.why: NSTEMI presents with evidence of myocardial necrosis (elevated troponin) along with ischemic symptoms. ST elevation is absent.
options.would_make_right: Change troponin to be clearly elevated (e.g., 0.9 ng/mL) while keeping ECG without ST elevation.

options.why: Unstable angina causes ischemic symptoms and ECG changes but does not elevate troponin because there is no measurable myocardial necrosis.
options.would_make_right: Set high-sensitivity troponin I to remain normal (e.g., 0.02 ng/mL) with the same ECG findings.

options.why: STEMI requires ST-segment elevation on ECG, which is explicitly not present here.
options.would_make_right: Modify the ECG description to include ST-segment elevation (e.g., ≥1 mm in contiguous leads) while keeping troponin elevated.

options.why: Acute pericarditis typically has diffuse, pleuritic pain and ECG changes such as diffuse ST elevation with PR depression, not regional ST depression plus troponin-defined NSTEMI.
options.would_make_right: Replace symptoms with pleuritic pain relieved by leaning forward and describe diffuse ST elevation with PR depression.

options.why: Pulmonary embolism may cause chest pain and tachycardia, but the vignette lacks supportive features (eg, hypoxemia, risk factors) and shows troponin elevation with ischemic ECG changes consistent with ACS.
options.would_make_right: Add hypoxemia and tachycardia with high clinical suspicion for PE (e.g., SpO2 90% and ECG showing S1Q3T3) while removing ischemic ECG pattern.

review.rule: In acute coronary syndrome, troponin presence distinguishes myocardial infarction (NSTEMI) from unstable angina when no ST elevation exists.
sources: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 - Cardiovascular System
ACC/AHA Guidelines for Acute Coronary Syndromes

review.hook: Low MCV always means thalassemia, not iron deficiency, right?
review.vignette: A 34-year-old woman presents with months of fatigue and pica. She reports heavy menstrual bleeding and dietary restriction. Vitals are T 37.0°C (98.6°F), HR 98/min, BP 112/70 mmHg, and SpO2 99% on room air. CBC shows hemoglobin 9.2 g/dL, MCV 68 fL, and RDW 18%. Peripheral smear demonstrates microcytosis and hypochromia. Iron studies reveal serum ferritin 6 ng/mL, serum iron 28 mcg/dL, and total iron-binding capacity 420 mcg/dL. What is the most likely diagnosis?
review.short_vignette: Woman with heavy menses: microcytic anemia (MCV 68), high RDW, low ferritin, low iron, high TIBC. Most likely diagnosis?
review.stem: Which diagnosis best explains her microcytic anemia pattern?

options.why: Low ferritin indicates depleted iron stores. Elevated TIBC with low serum iron supports iron deficiency rather than impaired globin synthesis.
options.would_make_right: Keep ferritin low (e.g., 6 ng/mL) and TIBC high; mention ongoing heavy menstrual bleeding would remain.

options.why: Thalassemia trait typically has normal or elevated iron stores and often a relatively normal RDW. Her iron studies show depleted stores.
options.would_make_right: Change ferritin to normal or high (e.g., 100 ng/mL) and make TIBC low/normal while keeping microcytosis.

options.why: Anemia of chronic inflammation usually shows low serum iron with low/normal TIBC due to increased hepcidin. Her TIBC is elevated.
options.would_make_right: Add a chronic inflammatory condition and change TIBC to low/normal with ferritin elevated (not 6 ng/mL).

options.why: Sideroblastic anemia is characterized by impaired heme synthesis and often increased iron stores. Her ferritin is markedly low.
options.would_make_right: Add ring sideroblasts on smear and change ferritin to elevated with higher iron and low TIBC.

options.why: Lead poisoning causes microcytosis and can show basophilic stippling, but iron stores are not depleted like in iron deficiency. The vignette lacks exposure and shows low ferritin.
options.would_make_right: Add relevant exposure (e.g., old paint renovation) and include basophilic stippling, while changing ferritin to normal.

review.rule: Microcytic anemia with low ferritin and high TIBC indicates iron deficiency, not thalassemia or inflammation.
sources: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 - Hematology (Anemia; Microcytic Anemias)

review.hook: After a viral illness, new neuro deficits suggest which demyelinating disease?
review.vignette: An 8-year-old boy presents 10 days after recovering from a febrile viral illness with sudden ataxia, dysarthria, and bilateral lower-extremity weakness. His temperature is 37.1°C. Vitals are stable. Exam shows truncal instability and increased reflexes with ankle clonus. Lumbar puncture reveals CSF with mild lymphocytic pleocytosis and elevated protein. MRI brain shows multiple nonenhancing, scattered white-matter lesions. He has no meningismus and no focal seizure activity.
review.short_vignette: Eight-year-old develops ataxia and weakness 10 days after viral illness; mild lymphocytic CSF; MRI shows multifocal white-matter demyelination.
review.stem: Which diagnosis best explains his symptoms and imaging pattern?

options.why: Typically occurs days to weeks after a viral infection via immune-mediated demyelination. MRI often shows multifocal white-matter lesions; CSF may show mild lymphocytic pleocytosis and elevated protein.
options.would_make_right: Add a 1–3-week post-viral timeline and multifocal nonenhancing white-matter lesions on MRI.

options.why: Bacterial meningitis usually presents with fever, meningismus, and CSF with marked neutrophilic pleocytosis and low glucose. His afebrile status and lack of meningismus argue against it.
options.would_make_right: Change the vignette to fever with meningismus and CSF neutrophils plus low glucose.

options.why: GBS causes ascending symmetric weakness and areflexia, often with nerve conduction abnormalities. This child has central signs (ataxia, clonus) suggesting CNS involvement rather than peripheral neuropathy.
options.would_make_right: Replace ataxia/clonus with progressive ascending weakness and absent reflexes, and add albuminocytologic dissociation in CSF.

options.why: Stroke would not classically follow a viral illness by days with multifocal demyelinating white-matter lesions. The CSF pattern here is mild inflammatory rather than focal vascular injury.
options.would_make_right: Add sudden unilateral deficits with vascular risk factors and MRI showing acute territorial infarction rather than multifocal demyelination.

options.why: Multiple sclerosis is less likely in an 8-year-old with a single monophasic post-infectious presentation. MS typically shows dissemination in time and space, often with enhancing lesions on MRI.
options.would_make_right: Add prior neurologic episodes separated over time and persistent new lesions to demonstrate dissemination in time.

review.rule: Post-infectious onset with multifocal demyelinating CNS lesions and mild inflammatory CSF suggests acute disseminated encephalomyelitis.
sources: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 - Neurologic Disorders
AAN guideline: demyelinating disorders clinical correlation

review.hook: He says, 'Only one test matters for pancreatitis,' but you must use the full diagnostic criteria.
review.vignette: A 42-year-old man presents with severe epigastric pain radiating to the back and nausea for 2 days. He drinks alcohol daily. Vitals: T 38.2 C (100.8 F), HR 102/min, BP 128/76 mm Hg. Exam shows epigastric tenderness without guarding. Labs show AST 70 U/L, ALT 65 U/L, and serum lipase 920 U/L (laboratory upper limit 200 U/L). Abdominal ultrasound shows gallstones. How should pancreatitis be diagnosed in this patient?
review.short_vignette: 42-year-old man with epigastric pain radiating to back; lipase 920 U/L with ULN 200; diagnosis requires key criteria—so which is best?
review.stem: Which finding best supports the diagnosis of acute pancreatitis?

options.why: Mild elevations of amylase can occur with many conditions and are not specific for acute pancreatitis. The diagnostic criterion requires lipase or amylase elevated to at least 3× the upper limit.
options.would_make_right: Change lipase to 920 U/L with ULN 200 while amylase remains only 1.5×; then amylase would not be the best supportive finding.

options.why: A 2× elevation does not meet the usual threshold used for diagnostic support. The criterion is at least 3× the upper limit in the appropriate clinical setting.
options.would_make_right: Lower the reported lipase to 400 U/L (2× ULN 200) while keeping symptoms; then pancreatitis would be less strongly supported.

options.why: Serum lipase is elevated to ≥3× the upper limit, which is a core diagnostic criterion for acute pancreatitis when consistent with symptoms.
options.would_make_right: Keep epigastric pain radiating to back and change lipase to ≥600 U/L (3× ULN 200), as in the vignette.

options.text: Normal serum lipase with mild epigastric tenderness
options.why: Normal pancreatic enzymes argue against acute pancreatitis, especially in the absence of imaging-confirming findings. Tenderness alone is not diagnostic.
options.would_make_right: Change lipase to normal and add imaging evidence of pancreatic inflammation; then imaging-based criteria could become best.

options.text: Gallstones on ultrasound without enzyme elevation
options.why: Gallstones can be present without pancreatitis. Diagnosis requires clinical features and/or enzyme elevation to meet diagnostic criteria.
options.would_make_right: Keep gallstones but raise lipase to ≥3× ULN; then enzyme elevation would support diagnosis as in the vignette.

review.rule: Acute pancreatitis is diagnosed when typical symptoms plus ≥3× upper-limit lipase/amylase and/or characteristic imaging findings are present.
sources: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 - GI Disorders
ACG guideline for acute pancreatitis (diagnostic criteria: 2 of 3)

review.topic: Hypothyroidism and Medication-Related Decreased GI Absorption
review.hook: A patient on levothyroxine develops constipation—stop thinking dose changes if meds interfere with absorption.
review.vignette: A 42-year-old woman has fatigue and weight gain for 6 weeks. Vitals are T 36.8 C, HR 74/min, BP 118/76 mmHg, RR 14/min. She was diagnosed with hypothyroidism 2 years ago and takes levothyroxine daily. Over the last month, she started taking calcium carbonate twice daily for dyspepsia. Labs show total T4 3.2 mcg/dL (normal 5-12), TSH 12.8 mIU/L (normal 0.4-4.5). She reports increased constipation but no heat intolerance, tremor, or palpitations. What is the most likely reason her levothyroxine is less effective?
review.short_vignette: Hypothyroid symptoms: T4 low, TSH high. New calcium carbonate started—what mechanism explains decreased levothyroxine effect?
review.stem: What is the most likely reason her levothyroxine is less effective?

options.text: Calcium binds levothyroxine in the gut, reducing absorption
options.why: Calcium can form insoluble complexes with levothyroxine in the gastrointestinal tract. This decreases bioavailability, leading to low T4 with compensatory elevated TSH.
options.would_make_right: Add a brief note that she takes levothyroxine and calcium carbonate at the same time each day.

options.text: Calcium stimulates thyroid hormone production, lowering TSH
options.why: The patient already has hypothyroidism and is taking replacement therapy. Calcium does not directly increase thyroid hormone synthesis to lower TSH.
options.would_make_right: Change labs to show high T4 with low TSH and include symptoms of hyperthyroidism.

options.text: Calcium increases hepatic clearance of levothyroxine
options.why: Hepatic clearance increases are better explained by enzyme-inducing drugs. The vignette points to an intestinal absorption issue rather than altered metabolism.
options.would_make_right: Replace calcium with a known hepatic enzyme inducer and specify timing consistent with enhanced metabolism.

options.text: Calcium decreases TSH secretion from the pituitary
options.why: If TSH secretion decreased, TSH would be low or normal rather than elevated in response to low T4.
options.would_make_right: Change TSH to be low (e.g., 0.2 mIU/L) while T4 is low or normal.

options.text: Calcium causes thyroid gland destruction, leading to hyperthyroidism
options.why: Gland destruction would not selectively produce hyperthyroidism in a chronic replacement scenario, and the labs show low T4 with high TSH.
options.would_make_right: Add acute onset of weight loss, tremor, and labs showing elevated T4 with suppressed TSH.

review.rule: In hypothyroid patients on levothyroxine, a new low T4 with high TSH suggests decreased hormone bioavailability or ineffective dosing schedule.
sources: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 - Endocrine (Thyroid Disease) and Pharmacology (Levothyroxine interactions)
American Thyroid Association patient counseling/medication administration guidance

review.hook: He got better after naloxone—what must the opioid have been doing first?
review.vignette: A 42-year-old man is found unresponsive after taking “pain pills.” Vitals show RR 6/min, O2 sat 88%, and BP 104/68 mmHg. Pupils are pinpoint. Capillary glucose is 98 mg/dL. After naloxone is administered, his respiratory rate rapidly improves to 16/min and oxygen saturation rises to 97% within minutes. The opioid effect wears off as naloxone competes at receptors. Which drug mechanism best explains this immediate reversal?
review.short_vignette: Opioid overdose with pinpoint pupils and hypoventilation improves rapidly after naloxone. What opioid receptor effect was being reversed?
review.stem: How does naloxone produce rapid improvement in opioid-induced respiratory depression?

options.why: Naloxone rapidly displaces opioids at μ-opioid receptors because it is a competitive antagonist. This restores normal respiratory drive quickly when the receptor is no longer occupied by the agonist.
options.would_make_right: Keep the same vignette, but add that the patient had opioids at high concentrations; naloxone would still restore breathing promptly by receptor competition.

options.why: Irreversible receptor damage would not explain rapid recovery within minutes. It would be unlikely to show quick, reversible physiologic improvement.
options.would_make_right: Change the vignette to show that recovery takes days and includes evidence of receptor loss (eg, no response to further naloxone), which is not present here.

options.text: Inhibition of hepatic CYP450 metabolism of opioids
options.why: Blocking metabolism would prolong opioid effects rather than rapidly reverse them. The expected outcome would be persistent hypoventilation.
options.would_make_right: Alter the vignette so naloxone worsens or does not improve respiratory depression; that would fit metabolism inhibition, not receptor antagonism.

options.why: GABA-A activation causes sedation and respiratory depression, not reversal of opioid-induced hypoventilation. It would worsen the presentation.
options.would_make_right: Modify the vignette so the patient becomes more somnolent and hypoventilates after the reversal agent, consistent with GABA-A potentiation.

options.text: Activation of cannabinoid receptors leading to respiratory stimulation
options.why: Cannabinoid receptor activation is not the mechanism of naloxone. In this vignette, the classic opioid toxidrome is present and is specifically reversed by opioid antagonism.
options.would_make_right: Change the vignette hook to explicitly describe synthetic cannabinoid intoxication without opioid signs; then a cannabinoid mechanism could be tested.

review.rule: Naloxone reverses opioid toxicity by competitively antagonizing μ-opioid receptors, rapidly restoring respiration when the receptor is displaced.
sources: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 - Pharmacology: Opioids & Antagonists
FDA/Drug label: Naloxone mechanism of action

review.hook: He asks why a drug helps tremor without fixing the underlying dopamine cell loss.
review.vignette: A 67-year-old man reports a 2-year history of resting tremor in his right hand and progressive stiffness when turning in bed. He has bradykinesia and cogwheel rigidity bilaterally, worse on the right. Vitals are T 36.8 C, HR 78/min, BP 128/74 mm Hg. He reports no history of stroke, and his cognition is intact. A clinician starts an oral medication to reduce tremor and improve movement. Which mechanism best explains the medication’s symptomatic benefit?
review.short_vignette: 67M with resting tremor, bradykinesia, cogwheel rigidity; intact cognition. Oral therapy started. Which mechanism explains symptomatic benefit?
review.stem: Which mechanism best explains the symptomatic benefit of therapy for his disorder?

options.text: Increases synaptic dopamine by inhibiting its breakdown
options.why: Parkinson disease is characterized by loss of dopaminergic neurons. Inhibiting dopamine breakdown increases available dopamine in the striatum, improving symptoms without reversing neuron loss.
options.would_make_right: Add a statement that the chosen medication is an MAO-B inhibitor and that symptoms improve as dopamine is preserved.

options.text: Blocks postsynaptic dopamine D2 receptors in the striatum
options.why: D2 receptor antagonism would worsen parkinsonian symptoms by reducing dopaminergic signaling, which contradicts symptomatic improvement in the vignette.
options.would_make_right: Change the vignette to describe symptom worsening after starting a dopamine antagonist (e.g., new antipsychotic).

options.text: Depletes dopamine via irreversible vesicular monoamine transporter inhibition
options.why: Depleting dopamine decreases motor control and would exacerbate tremor and rigidity rather than improving them.
options.would_make_right: Specify the medication irreversibly depletes vesicular dopamine, and adjust the vignette to worsening symptoms after initiation.

options.text: Promotes dopamine synthesis by increasing tyrosine hydroxylase activity
options.why: This mechanism is a different approach to raising dopamine, and the vignette does not provide clues that the therapy is a dopamine precursor strategy.
options.would_make_right: Replace the medication with a dopamine precursor (e.g., explicitly name levodopa) and state the patient has severe motor symptoms responsive to it.

options.text: Increases acetylcholine signaling by inhibiting acetylcholinesterase
options.why: Enhancing acetylcholine would worsen the dopamine–acetylcholine imbalance typical of Parkinson disease rather than treating tremor and rigidity.
options.would_make_right: State the medication is an acetylcholinesterase inhibitor and that he develops worsening rigidity.

review.rule: Parkinson disease symptoms improve when dopaminergic signaling in the striatum is increased, often by preventing dopamine breakdown.
sources: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 - Neurology/Movement Disorders
First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 - Pharmacology (Parkinson disease drugs: MAO-B inhibitors, levodopa, dopamine agonists)

review.hook: Atony is common, but which risk factors actually point you to genital tract laceration?
review.key_finding: Firm uterus; bright red heavy bleeding
review.vignette: A 28-year-old G2P2 woman is 2 hours postpartum after an uncomplicated vaginal delivery. She reports heavy vaginal bleeding and feeling lightheaded. Vitals are T 36.8°C, HR 118/min, BP 92/60 mmHg, RR 18/min. Exam shows brisk bright red bleeding from the vagina. The uterus is firm and well-contracted. Pelvic exam reveals pooling of blood with a suspected cervical laceration. She has no fever. Which etiology best explains her hemorrhage?
review.short_vignette: 2 hours postpartum with brisk bright red bleeding, firm uterus, and suspected cervical laceration.
review.stem: Which cause is most consistent with her postpartum hemorrhage presentation?

options.why: Uterine atony causes a boggy, poorly contracted uterus. Her uterus is firm and well-contracted.
options.would_make_right: Change exam to a boggy, enlarged uterus with poor tone despite uterine massage.

options.why: Active heavy bleeding with a firm uterus and suspected cervical/vaginal trauma indicates laceration-related hemorrhage.
options.would_make_right: Keep uterus firm and add a clearly visualized cervical or vaginal tear on speculum exam.

options.why: Retained products typically produce subinvolution with a boggy uterus and often abnormal bleeding patterns later postpartum.
options.would_make_right: Change uterus to boggy and add ultrasound evidence of retained placental tissue.

options.why: Uterine inversion causes an altered fundus position and severe pain during delivery, not a firm, well-contracted uterus.
options.would_make_right: Alter exam to show the fundus inverted into the vagina with acute severe pain.

options.why: Amniotic fluid embolism presents with sudden respiratory distress and shock accompanied by DIC, not isolated firm-uterus bleeding.
options.would_make_right: Add sudden hypoxia, frothy breathing, and prolonged PT/aPTT with low fibrinogen.

review.rule: In postpartum hemorrhage, a firm uterus points to genital trauma; a boggy uterus points to atony.
sources: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 - Obstetrics: Postpartum Hemorrhage
ACOG Practice Bulletin (postpartum hemorrhage evaluation)

review.hook: He wheezes after exercise—don’t confuse asthma with COPD or anaphylaxis.
review.vignette: A 19-year-old man with seasonal allergies reports 2 weeks of intermittent nighttime wheezing and chest tightness. Symptoms worsen with cold air and during a soccer match, then improve after using an inhaler. Vitals show T 36.8°C, HR 92/min, RR 22/min, BP 118/70 mmHg, and SpO2 96% on room air. Spirometry demonstrates reversible airflow obstruction. Serum studies show elevated IgE. Peripheral blood smear reveals eosinophilia. He has no fever, no productive cough, and no smoking history.
review.short_vignette: 19M with seasonal allergies has reversible wheeze after exercise; elevated IgE and eosinophilia point to allergic asthma.
review.stem: Which mechanism best explains his episodic wheezing?

options.text: IL-4 and IL-13 driven class switching to IgE in B cells
options.why: Allergic asthma is mediated by Th2 cytokines (IL-4/IL-13) that promote IgE class switching, leading to mast cell activation. This matches elevated IgE and eosinophilia with reversible obstruction.
options.would_make_right: Add a history of atopy with positive skin testing to a specific allergen and note mast cell–mediated immediate symptoms after allergen exposure.

options.text: Neutrophil elastase causing fixed airway destruction
options.why: Fixed airway destruction is characteristic of COPD/emphysema rather than asthma. His obstruction is reversible and eosinophilia with elevated IgE suggests allergic inflammation.
options.would_make_right: Change spirometry to show persistent obstruction with no reversibility after bronchodilator and add long smoking history with chronic productive cough.

options.text: IgG-mediated immune complex deposition in alveoli
options.why: Immune complex disease (often IgG) is associated with conditions like hypersensitivity pneumonitis or certain vasculitides, not typical episodic wheezing with reversible obstruction and atopy.
options.would_make_right: Replace wheezing episodes with progressive dyspnea and hypoxemia after a specific exposure, and include imaging consistent with alveolar infiltrates (e.g., ground-glass opacities).

options.text: Rapid mast-cell degranulation triggered by IgE cross-linking
options.why: IgE cross-linking can occur in allergic reactions, but the question asks for the mechanism best explaining his disease pattern given the decisive lab clue (elevated IgE with eosinophilia). The key immunologic driver is Th2 cytokine–mediated IgE class switching.
options.would_make_right: If you add an immediate onset of symptoms within minutes after allergen exposure and omit the elevated IgE/eosinophilia emphasis, then rapid mast-cell degranulation would become the best answer.

options.text: Destruction of alveolar septa from granulomatous inflammation
options.why: Granulomatous inflammation leading to septal destruction is not the mechanism of asthma. His reversible bronchospasm and atopic findings argue against a granulomatous process.
options.would_make_right: Introduce systemic symptoms (fever, night sweats), chest CT showing granulomas, and include labs suggesting sarcoidosis or another granulomatous disease.

review.rule: In allergic asthma, Th2 cytokines promote IgE production that triggers mast cells and eosinophilic airway inflammation.
sources: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 - Respiratory Disorders (Asthma)
GINA (allergic asthma/Th2–IgE pathophysiology)

review.hook: Do not confuse high free T4 from thyroid hormone resistance with primary hypothyroidism.
review.vignette: A 16-year-old girl has fatigue and poor concentration. Her mother reports she has always been “a little slowed,” and she started puberty on time. She takes no medications. Vitals are T 36.2°C, HR 58/min, and BP 108/70 mmHg. Labs show free T4 2.8 ng/dL (normal 0.8–1.8) and TSH 6.0 mIU/L (normal 0.4–4.0). Thyroid antibodies are negative. Which diagnosis best explains the discordant thyroid studies?
review.short_vignette: Teen with fatigue: free T4 high and TSH elevated. Antibodies negative. Not medication related—best diagnosis?
review.stem: Which diagnosis best explains elevated free T4 with an inappropriately high TSH?

options.why: In thyroid hormone resistance, peripheral tissues are less responsive to thyroid hormone, so feedback cannot suppress TSH despite elevated thyroid hormone levels. This produces high free T4 with nonsuppressed or elevated TSH.
options.would_make_right: Add family history of similar thyroid lab abnormalities with minimal symptoms despite high free T4.

options.text: Primary hypothyroidism due to thyroid failure
options.why: Primary hypothyroidism would cause low free T4 due to impaired thyroid hormone production. TSH is typically elevated in response, but free T4 should not be high.
options.would_make_right: Change free T4 to below the normal range (e.g., 0.5 ng/dL) while keeping TSH elevated.

options.why: Central hypothyroidism causes low or low-normal free T4 with inappropriately low or normal TSH. Elevated free T4 argues against pituitary failure causing insufficient thyroid stimulation.
options.would_make_right: Change TSH to low or normal (e.g., 0.6 mIU/L) while free T4 is low.

options.why: Toxic multinodular goiter causes excessive thyroid hormone production, leading to high free T4 and/or T3 with suppressed TSH via negative feedback. Here, TSH is elevated, which contradicts hyperthyroidism feedback physiology.
options.would_make_right: Suppress TSH to below normal (e.g., 0.1 mIU/L) while free T4 remains high.

options.text: Thyroid hormone ingestion from exogenous levothyroxine
options.why: Exogenous thyroid hormone increases free T4 and should suppress TSH through negative feedback. Persistent elevation of TSH indicates the feedback loop is not appropriately responding to circulating hormone.
options.would_make_right: Specify missed doses are impossible and add TSH suppression to below normal (e.g., 0.2 mIU/L).

review.rule: Discordant thyroid labs with high free T4 should suppress TSH unless tissues or the feedback system are resistant.
sources: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 - Endocrine
American Thyroid Association (patient and clinician educational summaries on thyroid hormone resistance)

review.topic: Microcytic Anemia: Thalassemia Versus Iron Deficiency
review.hook: Don’t assume all microcytosis is iron deficiency—look at the RDW and RBC count.
review.vignette: A 27-year-old man presents for evaluation of long-standing fatigue. He denies melena and has no pica. Vitals are normal: T 36.8 C, HR 78/min, BP 118/72 mmHg, SpO2 99% on room air. CBC shows: Hb 10.8 g/dL, Hct 33%, MCV 62 fL, RDW 13%, RBC count 6.1 million/µL, platelets 260,000/µL. Iron studies are normal with ferritin 95 ng/mL and transferrin saturation 32%. Which diagnosis best explains the microcytosis?
review.short_vignette: Fatigue with Hb 10.8, MCV 62, RDW 13%, high RBC count, normal ferritin and saturation—most consistent with thalassemia.
review.stem: Which diagnosis best explains this patient’s microcytosis?

options.why: Iron deficiency classically causes elevated RDW and low ferritin/transferrin saturation. Here, ferritin and saturation are normal, arguing against iron deficiency.
options.would_make_right: Change ferritin to 10 ng/mL and transferrin saturation to 10%, and increase RDW to 18%.

options.why: Thalassemia trait causes microcytosis with a relatively normal RDW and often a normal or elevated RBC count, with normal iron studies.
options.would_make_right: Keep ferritin and transferrin saturation normal; also raise Hb slightly (e.g., 11.5 g/dL) while preserving low MCV and normal RDW.

options.why: Sideroblastic anemia is associated with impaired heme synthesis and often elevated RDW with iron overload; iron studies would not be normal in a way that explains isolated microcytosis here.
options.would_make_right: Add iron overload pattern (e.g., elevated serum iron and transferrin saturation) and note increased ring sideroblasts on marrow.

options.why: Anemia of chronic inflammation typically shows low serum iron with normal or increased ferritin and usually presents in the setting of chronic disease rather than isolated normal iron studies.
options.would_make_right: Introduce a chronic inflammatory condition and make transferrin saturation low (e.g., 12%) with ferritin elevated (e.g., 250 ng/mL).

options.why: Lead poisoning can cause microcytosis, but the vignette lacks exposure history and would be expected to show additional findings such as basophilic stippling and abnormal iron handling.
options.would_make_right: Add occupational exposure to lead-based paint and include basophilic stippling on peripheral smear with elevated blood lead level.

review.rule: In microcytic anemia, normal iron studies plus low RDW and normal/high RBC count favors thalassemia trait over iron deficiency.
sources: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 - Hematology/Anemias
USPSTF/clinical diagnostic approach to microcytic anemia (general)

review.hook: This patient’s symptoms improve, but ask what drug target is blocked, not acid output alone.
review.vignette: A 58-year-old man with epigastric burning and GERD takes omeprazole daily. Over the next several days, his symptoms improve and his gastric pH rises. He asks why the medication works even though he has no immediate relief right after the first dose. Vitals are normal. An endoscopy shows reflux esophagitis. A gastric sample taken 24 hours after the last dose shows markedly reduced activity of the proton pump in parietal cells compared with baseline. Which process is directly inhibited by omeprazole?
review.short_vignette: GERD improved days into therapy; gastric sampling shows reduced proton pump activity—mechanism involves irreversible inhibition.
review.stem: What process is directly inhibited by omeprazole in parietal cells?

options.text: H+/K+ ATPase in gastric parietal cells
options.why: Omeprazole irreversibly inhibits the luminal H+/K+ ATPase, shutting down final common pathway for gastric acid secretion. The clinical effect improves after parietal cells regenerate, explaining delayed maximal symptom relief.
options.would_make_right: Change the vignette to state that parietal cell H+/K+ ATPase activity is irreversibly decreased with omeprazole exposure.

options.text: Histamine H2 receptors on parietal cells
options.why: H2 blockers reduce acid via decreased cAMP signaling, but they do not irreversibly inhibit the ATPase pump. The vignette emphasizes proton pump activity specifically being reduced.
options.would_make_right: Change the vignette to show decreased histamine-driven cAMP signaling at the H2 receptor without mention of ATPase activity reduction.

options.text: Carbonic anhydrase in gastric parietal cells
options.why: Carbonic anhydrase inhibitors reduce formation of bicarbonate and affect acid generation, but they are not the mechanism of omeprazole. The key finding points to the final proton pump.
options.would_make_right: Change the vignette to mention decreased CO2 hydration (carbonic anhydrase activity) affecting bicarbonate production.

options.text: Gastrin receptor signaling via increased cAMP
options.why: Gastrin receptor blockade is not the direct target of PPIs. The vignette describes direct reduction in the proton pump, not altered gastrin-mediated second messenger pathways.
options.would_make_right: Change the vignette to document blockade of gastrin receptors and restored cAMP dynamics rather than reduced ATPase activity.

options.why: Muscarinic antagonists reduce acid by blocking acetylcholine on parietal cells, not by irreversibly inhibiting the H+/K+ ATPase. The stem’s emphasis is on proton pump activity.
options.would_make_right: Change the vignette to show that acetylcholine-driven muscarinic signaling is blocked with unchanged proton pump ATPase activity.

review.rule: PPIs irreversibly inhibit the gastric H+/K+ ATPase, the final common pathway for acid secretion.
sources: First Aid for the USMLE Step 1 - Pharmacology (Proton Pump Inhibitors)
Gastroesophageal Reflux Disease pharmacology review (final common pathway acid secretion)
